implementation_notes: A plain aggregate struct with public, owned members replaces the accessor-heavy bean: no getters, no vtable, no invariants to violate, and aggregate initialisation keeps construction cheap. Serialization is supplied by the codec library through ADL to_json/from_json overloads (nlohmann::json) or an equivalent serializer, so the DTO stays a plain value type and the wire shape lives in one function pair. Choose this default when the payload crosses a JSON/REST boundary and adding a code-generation step is not justified.
pitfalls: Serializing through pointers or polymorphic bases slices objects and can leave dangling references; a DTO should own its members or hold views into a buffer that outlives it.
string_view/span members make the DTO non-owning and easily dangling on return; decide and document ownership per field.
Without an explicit field mapping a serializer walks every public member, so adding a member silently changes the wire contract.

variants.name: IDL-generated message class (protobuf / FlatBuffers)
variants.implementation_notes: Schema-first realization: the .proto/.fbs file is the source of truth and protoc or flatc generate the DTO class together with its encode/decode code; field numbers carry the versioning contract, so additive changes stay compatible across languages. The generated class replaces the hand-written carrier entirely, and the price is a build-time code-generation step plus a schema governed as its own artifact. FlatBuffers is the zero-copy variant of the same idea: generated accessors read directly from the buffer without unpacking, at the cost of a read-only, more rigid object model.
pitfalls: Generated classes are still transport types: letting them into the domain couples business code to the schema and to the protobuf build/runtime.
Field numbers are permanent: reusing or renumbering a tag breaks old readers silently - no error, just wrong data.
FlatBuffers payloads are read-only views over a buffer that must outlive every accessor, unlike a protobuf message, which owns its data.
